content:
Multiple legal and business groups, together with the U.S. government, filed briefs with the Supreme Court this week urging justices to overturn at least part of a civil contempt finding against Apple in its ongoing case with Epic Games. Details below.

A little background

In late June, the U.S. Supreme Court agreed to hear Apple's appeal, arguing that a civil contempt finding against it in its case with Epic Games should be vacated.

In short, when Apple was ordered by the court to allow developers to steer users to outside purchasing options, Apple complied but charged a 27% commission on those transactions. Epic later challenged Apple's compliance, and a district court found Apple in civil contempt.

Apple has since allowed developers to link to outside purchasing options without charging a commission.

Apple has been trying to overturn that finding ever since, arguing that the actual text of the injunction did not prohibit it from charging a commission, and that the lower court improperly relied on the "spirit of the injunction" in finding it in contempt.

For reference, the original order read as follows:

Last week, Apple officially filed its main brief with the Supreme Court, again arguing that the contempt finding should be overturned because the original injunction didn't explicitly prohibit it from charging a commission on purchases made outside the App Store.

In the brief, Apple also argued that letting the contempt finding stand would increase the risk of courts overstepping when enforcing injunctions, making it difficult for companies to know exactly what an order prohibits.

U.S. government and other groups weigh in

Epic Games is required to file its response brief by November 13, but the Supreme Court has already received multiple amicus briefs this week — submitted by outside interested parties — from the U.S. Department of Justice, filed through the Office of the Deputy Solicitor General, along with several legal and business groups weighing in on Apple's appeal.

The DOJ argued in its amicus brief that "civil contempt is only appropriate when the defendant's conduct is plainly within the scope of the injunction's express terms," and noted that Apple's decision to charge a 27% commission doesn't fall into that category.

The brief went on to echo Apple's argument that as long as there is a "reasonable doubt" about whether an injunction actually prohibits a behavior, there shouldn't be a finding of civil contempt, and concluded that the Supreme Court should "vacate the contempt finding as it relates to the 27% commission."

However, in that same brief, the DOJ also said that the lower court was correct in finding Apple in contempt for its "link-only" restriction, arguing the injunction specifically required Apple to allow both buttons and links, but Apple's compliance only allowed links.

For other disputed issues — such as restrictions on where external purchase links can appear — the DOJ said the Supreme Court should vacate the existing ruling and send the case back to the lower court to reconsider under the "reasonable doubt" standard.

In addition to the DOJ, the Supreme Court received amicus briefs from the following organizations:

  • U.S. Chamber of Commerce
  • Chamber of Progress
  • Former Federal Antitrust Enforcers
  • International Center for Law and Economics (ICLE)
  • Computer & Communications Industry Association (CCIA), NetChoice, and the Software & Information Industry Association (SIIA)
  • Washington Legal Foundation (WLF)

Generally speaking, they all backed a similar overall argument: that Apple should not be found in civil contempt for behavior an injunction didn't explicitly prohibit, and that courts should enforce injunctions based on their actual text, not some perceived "spirit."

ICLE added that "profitable compliance is still compliance," while the Former Federal Antitrust Enforcers cited past precedent to argue that having a judge decide how much commission Apple can charge "is exactly the kind of 'direct rate regulation' that antitrust courts typically avoid."

For now, a district court is in the process of determining how much (if any) commission Apple can charge for purchases linked to outside the App Store, while the Supreme Court is reviewing the contempt finding itself.
